strengths: Impressive headline result: MARC matches the 64-frame Qwen2.5-VL-3B baseline on mean benchmark score (42.20 vs 42.21) while using only ~4.7% of the visual tokens, with consistent gains over several training-free compression baselines (ByteVideoLLM, MovieChat, VidCom) under matched token budgets.

The retrieve-then-compress framing is sensible, and the paper includes useful ablations: comparison against SFT and SFT+VMR variants (Table 2), sensitivity analysis of the retention threshold τ (Table 3), and an isolation of VMR's contribution without training.
Efficiency evaluation is conducted on real hardware (A6000) reporting GPU peak memory (72.4% reduction) and latency breakdowns, rather than only reporting token counts.
The C-GRPO reward design (retention ratio gated by correctness) is clearly motivated and reasonably well specified, including the group-normalized advantage and KL-anchored objective.
weaknesses: The central claim is confounded by the retrieval component. Table 2 shows that untrained Qwen2.5-VL-3B with VMR at 64 frames achieves 45.56 — well above both the baseline (42.21) and full MARC (42.20). Thus the headline 'nearly identical accuracy' result appears driven primarily by query-aware clip retrieval, not by the RL compression itself; the trained student actually underperforms the simple retrieval baseline. The paper's narrative that C-GRPO enables 'teacher-level reasoning under extreme compression' is not clearly supported by this comparison.

Unfair comparison setup: VMR uses the query to select top-k clips before compression, whereas the compared compression baselines (MovieChat, VidCom, ByteVideoLLM) are query-agnostic. Query-conditioned frame selection is a known strong baseline, so the advantage over competing compression methods is partly attributable to extra information access rather than the compression algorithm.

Novelty is incremental: the temporal compression layer is explicitly an extension of cosine-similarity frame merging in the spirit of MovieChat/ToMe, and C-GRPO is standard GRPO plus one additional reward term. The 'first RL strategy for video token compression' claim is overstated given the close connection to existing RL distillation and reward-shaping work.

Manuscript quality issues: a broken cross-reference ('Appendix ??'), an inconsistent baseline name (text cites 'DynamicVLM' while Table 1 lists 'ByteVideoLLM'), broken formatting in the table ('VidCom2-3B'), and key details (retrieval index construction, event segmentation hyperparameters, retrieval overhead at inference) deferred to appendices that are not present in the reviewed manuscript.

Retrieval cost and failure modes are unaddressed: VMR requires encoding/indexing the full video and a query at inference, but the efficiency comparison counts only LLM-side memory/latency; no end-to-end cost of the retrieval stage is reported. Queries requiring global/spatial context (e.g., parts of VSI-Bench, VideoMME long videos, where the model retains only 74% of baseline) may be poorly served by top-3 clip retrieval, and this limitation is under-analyzed.

Potential benchmark contamination: the training set draws from public QA datasets (STAR, CLEVRER, NeXT-QA, PerceptionTest) whose task types overlap with evaluation benchmarks such as MVBench; the paper does not discuss de-duplication or contamination checks, which is especially important given that gains are partly attributed to 'enhanced instruction-following ability' from training.

Generalization is narrow: results are on a single 3B backbone; no scaling experiments, no statistical significance or variance reporting, and the reported latency reduction (23.9% LLM latency, 11.1% end-to-end) is modest relative to the 95% token reduction, which deserves more careful analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (extreme visual token compression for video LLMs) and reports results across six widely used benchmarks (VSI-Bench, VideoMMMU, MMVU, MVBench, TempCompass, VideoMME), which is broader evaluation than many compression papers.

The two-stage design (query-relevant event retrieval followed by RL-based distillation/compression) is a reasonable and coherent idea, and C-GRPO's retention-alignment reward gated by correctness is a sensible mechanism to prevent reward hacking.
Ablations cover the main components: VMR alone vs. C-GRPO, SFT vs. RL distillation, and the reward threshold τ, providing some evidence that both components contribute.
The method achieves a 95% token reduction (2589.93 → 122.69 tokens) while retaining near-baseline mean accuracy, and reports concrete memory/latency measurements on real hardware.
weaknesses: Confounded headline comparison. Table 2 shows that VMR alone with 64 frames scores 45.56 vs. 42.21 for the baseline, while the full MARC achieves only 42.20. This reveals (a) compression actually loses ~3.4 points relative to the retrieval-augmented model, and (b) the 'nearly identical to baseline' claim is partly driven by retrieval boosting scores on some benchmarks rather than by lossless compression. Baselines in Table 1 do not receive the same retrieval module, making the main comparison unfair; a retrieval-equipped baseline (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-3B + VMR at matched token budgets) is the proper comparator.

Overstated claims hide large per-benchmark drops. 'Nearly identical mean performance (42.20 vs. 42.21)' masks severe degradation on VSI-Bench (27.55 vs. 32.93, −16%) and VideoMME (39.44 vs. 53.55, −26%), which is problematic for the claimed deployment scenarios (long videos, autonomous driving). The mean parity is within noise; no statistical significance tests, error bars, or multiple seeds are reported.

Novelty is limited and the 'first RL strategy for video token compression' claim is questionable. VMR is largely an assembly of existing tools (TransNetV2 event segmentation + off-the-shelf embedding retrieval, both cited as external components), the temporal compression layer is explicitly an extension of cosine-similarity frame merging 'in the spirit of MovieChat', and C-GRPO is GRPO with one additional reward term (Eq. 7-8). The cognitive-science motivation reads as post-hoc dressing rather than a technical contribution.

Inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine confidence: a broken reference 'Appendix ??' appears in a main section; 'DynamicVLM' is cited for a 65% improvement but does not appear anywhere in Table 1 or the reference list; 'VideoMMU' vs. 'VideoMMMU' typos; the efficiency numbers are internally inconsistent (text claims 23.9% generation latency reduction, but Figure 6 shows LLM latency 2.51→2.11 s ≈ 15.9%); and 'top_p = 0.001 and temperature = 0.01 to achieve greedy decoding' is technically incoherent.

Potential benchmark contamination. Figure 4 shows the training set includes STAR, CLEVRER, NeXT-QA, and PerceptionTest data, which overlap in source content with MVBench tasks and other evaluation sets. The paper does not discuss or rule out test-set leakage, which is a serious validity concern given the gains on MVBench (+27.85% from VMR alone is also suspicious).

Efficiency evaluation is narrow and incomplete: a single benchmark (MMVU), single GPU type, one batch size, and only the 3B model. The end-to-end latency gain (11.1%) is modest, and the additional cost of running VMR (segmentation, embedding, NN search) at inference time is never accounted for.

Narrow scope and incomplete ablations: only one backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) is actually trained with C-GRPO despite other models being listed; no analysis of how performance varies with video length, number of retrieved clips k, or compression ratio ρ; the promised τ sensitivity analysis and VideoMME failure analysis are deferred to broken/missing appendices.

Reproducibility is weak: key training details (hyperparameters, reward scales α, KL coefficient, training compute) are relegated to appendices that appear broken or missing, and no code release is mentioned.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: visual token compression for video LLMs is practically important, and the retrieve-then-compress pipeline (VMR + RL-based compression) is a sensible decomposition.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: six benchmarks spanning reasoning and general video understanding, plus efficiency measurements (GPU memory, latency) with a matched-token-budget comparison against training-free baselines (MovieChat, VidCom, ByteVideoLLM).
Useful ablations: comparison of C-GRPO against SFT and SFT+VMR, sensitivity analysis of the retention threshold τ, and an isolation of VMR's contribution.
Reported efficiency gains (72% memory reduction, ~24% generation latency reduction) are meaningful for resource-constrained deployment.
weaknesses: The headline claim ('nearly identical accuracy to the 64-frame baseline') is framed against a weak uniform-sampling baseline, but the paper's own Table 2 shows VMR alone at 64 frames achieves 45.56 mean, well above MARC's 42.20. This means the trained compressed model actually loses ~3.4 points relative to the retrieval-only configuration, so the compression component (C-GRPO) appears to trade away accuracy rather than preserve teacher-level performance; the fair comparison is obscured by the presentation.

The comparison between MARC (which uses query-based retrieval at test time) and baselines that do not use retrieval raises fairness concerns; part of MARC's gain is attributable to VMR, which is orthogonal to token compression and could be added to any baseline.

Technical novelty is limited: the temporal merging layer is essentially cosine-similarity frame merging in the spirit of MovieChat/ToMe with a two-stage schedule, and C-GRPO is standard GRPO augmented with one extra gated reward term (Eq. 7-8). The 'first RL post-training compression strategy' claim is overstated without a careful survey of related RL-based pruning/distillation work.

The near-identical mean (42.20 vs 42.21) is well within run-to-run noise; no statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple seeds are reported, so the central 'parity' claim is not statistically supported.

Performance is inconsistent across benchmarks: VideoMME retains only 74% of baseline, and the method is evaluated only on a single 3B backbone (Qwen2.5-VL), leaving generality to other models/architectures unverified despite claims of broad applicability.

Writing and consistency problems undermine confidence: a broken reference ('Appendix ??'), the text discusses improvements over 'DynamicVLM' while Table 1 lists 'ByteVideoLLM-3B' with the same citation key, and the decoding setup ('top_p = 0.001 and temperature = 0.01 to achieve greedy decoding') is imprecise.

Key implementation details (retriever training, compression budget calibration, appendix content) are deferred, and the cognitive-science motivation for VMR is decorative rather than testable — the actual VMR is an off-the-shelf segmenter (TransNetV2) plus an embedding model.

Several claims lack supporting evidence in the main text (e.g., 'mitigating hallucination', attribution of TempCompass gains to instruction following), and the sensitivity of results to the number of retrieved clips (top-k=3) is not ablated.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: extreme visual token compression for video LLMs, with a clear retrieve-then-compress decomposition (event segmentation + retrieval, then RL-based distillation to a single-frame token budget).

The C-GRPO formulation is reasonable: the retention-alignment reward gated by correctness (Eqs. 6-10) is a sensible way to couple student compressed-input performance to a full-frame teacher while discouraging reward hacking.

Evaluation covers six widely used video benchmarks, includes comparisons against multiple training-free compression baselines (ByteVideoLLM, MovieChat, VidCom) at a matched token budget (~120 tokens), and includes SFT-based training comparisons plus τ ablations (Table 3) and a VMR ablation (Table 2).
The paper is transparent about failure modes (Appendix A.4), showing VideoMME degradation and diagnosing why retrieval to top-3 clips hurts long videos.
Efficiency results are concretely reported (72% GPU memory reduction, latency figures, peak token counts per benchmark in Table 4), with reproduction details in appendices.
weaknesses: The headline claim ('nearly identical accuracy to the 64-frame baseline') is confounded and partially misleading. Table 2 shows that the training-free VMR alone at 64 frames achieves 45.56 mean, clearly beating the full MARC-3B (42.20) and the baseline (42.21). The parity with baseline is thus largely attributable to query-aware frame/clip selection at test time (an oracle-like input selection), not to the compression itself; the compression stage still costs roughly 3.4 points relative to uncompressed VMR. The claim that compression 'maintains performance' overstates the evidence.

Mean-score parity masks severe, uneven behavior: MARC drops to 74% of baseline on VideoMME (39.44 vs 53.55) and loses 5+ points on VSI-Bench, while gaining implausibly large margins on TempCompass (+17 points) that the paper attributes to generic instruction-following benefits of training rather than compression — suggesting distribution-shift effects rather than genuine video-understanding preservation. The method is effectively a short/medium-clip method, which narrows its claimed scope for 'video understanding'.

Limited technical novelty. VMR is composed of existing off-the-shelf components (TransNetV2 shot detection + contrastive embedding retrieval); the temporal compression layer is essentially cosine-similarity frame merging in the spirit of MovieChat; C-GRPO is a modest reward-shaping modification of standard GRPO. The cognitive-science/episodic-memory framing is largely narrative and is not validated experimentally.
RL training for the student is done on only 5K samples, single seeds, no variance or significance reporting, while key conclusions rest on very small differences (42.20 vs 42.21 mean).

Efficiency numbers understate overhead: event segmentation, embedding, retrieval, and re-encoding of retrieved clips occur at inference, but the reported latency breakdown (23.9% LLM latency, 11.1% end-to-end) does not clearly isolate or justify preprocessing costs; latency reduction is modest relative to the 95% token reduction claimed.
The compression method is only demonstrated on Qwen2.5-VL-3B; other models (Gemma, InternVL) appear only as uncompressed references, leaving generality of C-GRPO across architectures unverified.

Missing discussion/comparison with stronger learned token-compression approaches (e.g., Q-Former-style learned compressors, RL-trained token pruning), and top-k=3 is fixed without sensitivity analysis despite acknowledged sensitivity on long videos.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (visual token cost of video VLMs) and the retrieve-then-compress pipeline is clearly described and mostly reproducible, with implementation details, prompts, and training hyperparameters provided in the appendix.

Experiments cover six benchmarks and include ablations of the main components (VMR, SFT vs. C-GRPO, the retention threshold τ), plus an honest failure-case analysis (Appendix A.4) acknowledging the 74% retention on VideoMME for long videos.
The efficiency measurements (GPU memory, latency) are conducted under matched token budgets for the compression baselines, which is a fair-comparison effort.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The VMR is a pipeline of off-the-shelf components (TransNetV2 shot detection + Perception Encoder embeddings + nearest-neighbor retrieval), and the temporal compression layer is explicitly a two-stage extension of cosine-similarity frame merging from MovieChat/ToMe. C-GRPO is essentially standard GRPO plus one additional gated reward term (Eq. 8), so the claim of proposing 'for the first time' a new RL compression strategy overstates a small delta over existing algorithms.

A crucial baseline is missing: plain Qwen2.5-VL-3B with uniformly sampled 1 frame (or 2-4 frames). Given that MVBench and TempCompass contain mostly short videos, a trivial uniform 1-frame baseline could achieve similar scores, which would undermine the headline claim that the 95% compression 'retains' baseline performance.

The headline result (42.20 vs. 42.21) appears to be driven primarily by VMR retrieval rather than by the RL compression: Table 2 shows VMR alone at 64 frames achieves 45.56, i.e., the full MARC pipeline actually loses 3.3 points relative to its own retrieval component. Meanwhile, the compression baselines are denied this retrieval advantage, making the comparisons and the narrative somewhat misleading.

The core claim of matching a 64-frame teacher with one frame's tokens is contradicted on long videos, where only 74% of baseline performance is retained; the abstract and introduction present near-parity as a general property. No statistical significance, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported, and a 0.01-point mean difference is well within run-to-run noise.

The efficiency gains are underwhelming and not fully explained: despite a 95% token reduction, generation latency drops only 23.9% and end-to-end latency only 11.1%, suggesting large unaccounted retrieval/compression overhead that undermines the deployment story for latency-sensitive applications.

The cognitive-science and neuroimaging motivation is decorative: no element of the method (contrastive retrieval, frame averaging, GRPO reward) is meaningfully tied to episodic memory, so this framing adds no scientific content.

Reward design details are incomplete: how a_full (the teacher's average reward) is estimated online during training, and how the retention ratio is computed across a group, are not specified; this is central to C-GRPO's behavior and reproducibility.

Writing and internal consistency issues: the paper asserts τ=0.6 was 'validated by ablations' before presenting them; contributions are described as 'threefold' with partially redundant items; key results are stated in inconsistent relative vs. absolute terms (e.g., '65%', '31%', '52%' improvements over baselines are actually point differences of 16.7, 10.1, and 14.4 on the mean).

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem (computational cost of video tokens in VLMs) with a sensible retrieve-then-compress design combining event-level retrieval (VMR) with RL-based distillation (C-GRPO).

The main result is impressive at the system level: near-baseline mean accuracy (42.20 vs 42.21) using only ~4.7% of visual tokens, with a 72% GPU memory reduction, evaluated across six diverse benchmarks.
The paper includes several useful ablations: comparison against SFT-based compression, sensitivity to the retention threshold τ, and isolation of the VMR contribution.

Baseline comparisons are carefully equalized (all compression baselines operating at ~120 tokens on the same backbone), and failure cases on long videos (VideoMME) are analyzed honestly in Appendix A.4.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: detailed prompts, training hyperparameters, dataset composition, and efficiency protocol are provided in appendices, with code/models promised.
weaknesses: The central claim is partly confounded by the VMR component. Table 2 shows that VMR alone (untrained, 64 frames) achieves 45.56 mean — higher than MARC-3B (42.20) and the baseline (42.21). Thus the headline 'matches the 64-frame baseline with 95% fewer tokens' is achieved because retrieval adds ~3.4 points that mask the true cost of compression. The paper's framing obscures that compression itself still loses performance relative to the best VMR configuration, and MARC is not compared against VMR at reduced frame counts (e.g., 8-16 frames with VMR), which is the most natural and missing strong baseline.

Fairness concerns in main comparisons: MARC is the only method that uses VMR (top-3 clip retrieval), while all compression baselines (MovieChat, VidCom, ByteVideoLLM) operate without retrieval. The reported relative improvements (65%, 31%, 52%) therefore conflate retrieval gains with compression quality.

Limited technical novelty: the individual components are largely existing — TransNetV2 for segmentation, Perception Encoder embeddings, ANN search, cosine-similarity frame merging essentially from MovieChat-style ToMe, and GRPO with one added reward term (Eq. 7-8) plus correctness gating. The claim that C-GRPO is 'the first' post-training RL strategy for video token compression is overclaimed and insufficiently supported against prior RL-based token pruning work. The cognitive-science motivation is decorative rather than technically operationalized.

No statistical significance or variance reporting. The key headline (42.20 vs 42.21) is a 0.01 difference well within run-to-run noise, and multiple-benchmark jumps (e.g., TempCompass 38.05 → 55.34) are attributed to generic 'instruction-following ability' without ruling out train/test overlap given the training data is drawn from many public QA datasets.

Efficiency gains are weaker than the headline suggests: only 23.9% generation latency and 11.1% end-to-end reduction, and the added VMR inference overhead (segmentation + embedding + retrieval) is not measured or included in end-to-end cost. The 72% memory reduction largely follows trivially from sequence-length reduction.

Single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) for all training and main results; generalization of C-GRPO to other architectures (InternVL, Gemma) is claimed in spirit but never demonstrated by training on a second backbone.
τ ablation covers only three values, and the method has several interacting hyperparameters (k, ρ, m, α, τ) with limited sensitivity analysis.

Presentation issues: 'contributions are threefold' typo, inconsistent method naming (DynamicVLM vs ByteVideoLLM in Sec 4.2 vs Table 1), a confusing footnote on the 'Frames' column, and rough figure formatting (Figure 5) suggest the paper would benefit from another careful pass.
